name: Twin Earth
statement: On a planet identical to ours except that water is a different chemical, the word water would mean something different, though nothing in anyone's head has changed.
statementAccent: though nothing in anyone's head has changed
meaning: Twin Earth is a thought experiment devised by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in his 1975 paper The Meaning of Meaning to argue that the meaning of words is not fixed purely by what is in a speaker's mind. Imagine a planet, Twin Earth, exactly like ours down to the last detail, with a duplicate of every person, except that the clear, drinkable liquid its inhabitants call water is not H2O but a different compound with the chemical formula abbreviated XYZ, indistinguishable in everyday experience. Back before anyone knew any chemistry, an Earthling and their Twin Earth double would be in identical mental states when they used the word water, yet the Earthling's word refers to H2O and the Twin's refers to XYZ. So the two words differ in meaning and reference despite the speakers being mentally identical. Putnam concluded, in his famous phrase, that meanings just ain't in the head.
mechanism: The argument isolates reference from psychology. Take an Earthling, Oscar, and his molecule-for-molecule mental duplicate on Twin Earth, both in 1750, before chemistry could tell H2O from XYZ. Their inner states, beliefs, and associations tied to water are identical. Yet what Oscar's word water picks out is the actual stuff around him, H2O, while his twin's word picks out XYZ. Because the words refer to different substances, they differ in meaning, even though the speakers' internal states do not differ at all. Meaning and reference must therefore depend in part on the external environment, on the actual nature of the stuff a term is used to track, and on a linguistic community's connection to it, not on inner mental content alone. This is the thesis of semantic externalism, captured in Putnam's slogan meanings ain't in the head, and it fits his view that natural-kind terms like water are fixed by the world's hidden structure, discovered by science, rather than by a description in the speaker's mind.

examples.text: Earth's water is H2O and Twin Earth's is XYZ, superficially identical; the same word water refers to different substances on the two planets.
An Earthling and their Twin Earth double, before chemistry, are in the same mental state using water, yet their words mean and refer to different things.
Putnam's conclusion that since reference depends on the external substance, the meaning of a natural-kind term is not fixed by the speaker's inner state alone.

variants.name: Semantic externalism
variants.text: The general view the experiment supports, that the meaning and reference of at least some terms are partly determined by factors outside the speaker's mind.

variants.name: The division of linguistic labour
variants.text: Putnam's related idea that a community relies on experts to fix the reference of natural-kind terms, so no individual need carry the full meaning in mind.

whyItMatters: Twin Earth is one of the most influential thought experiments in the philosophy of language and mind, the founding argument for semantic externalism. By showing that molecular twins could mean different things by the same word, it overturned the long-standing assumption that meaning is wholly a matter of what is in the head, reshaping theories of reference, mental content, and natural-kind terms. Its influence reaches into debates over whether the contents of thought, and not just of words, depend on the environment, bearing on questions about self-knowledge and the individuation of mental states. As a crisp, memorable scenario, it turned an abstract thesis about meaning into a vivid test case that has structured decades of argument about how language connects to the world.

working.lead: Fix the speakers' minds as identical
working.text: set the scenario before chemistry, so an Earthling and their twin are in the same inner state when they say water.
note that their words still refer to different substances, so meaning depends on the environment, not on inner content alone.

limits: Twin Earth argues that the meaning of natural-kind terms like water is not fixed by inner mental states alone; how far the lesson generalises is debated, and critics question whether it extends to all words or only to natural-kind and indexical terms. Some philosophers resist the intuition that the twins mean different things, or distinguish narrow content, shared by the twins, from wide content that differs, preserving a role for internal states. The scenario is also an idealisation, since a world with a water-like XYZ raises questions about how identical the two planets could really be. So the experiment establishes a powerful case for externalism about certain terms rather than a fully settled theory of all meaning, and its scope remains actively contested.
misreadings: The point is not a chemistry puzzle about exotic liquids but a claim about meaning: that reference can differ while inner states are the same, so meaning is not wholly in the head. It does not show that nothing about meaning is mental, only that the external environment partly fixes the reference of natural-kind terms. And it is not uncontested; philosophers debate whether the intuition holds and whether a notion of narrow, internally fixed content survives, so citing Twin Earth as proving all meaning is external overstates its reach.
origin: Introduced by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in his 1975 paper The Meaning of Meaning to argue for semantic externalism, the view that meaning and reference depend partly on the external world, summed up in his slogan that meanings ain't in the head.
